final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. The husband's best recourse runs through the immigration court. He should promptly file a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia removal order based on lack of notice, under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). That motion has no deadline and no filing fee, and filing it automatically stays removal. If it is granted, the proceedings are restarted and he can renew his I-485 before the immigration judge (IJ). He can also try to repair the I-130 with USCIS or by filing a new I-130.

1. WHAT TO FILE WITH THE IMMIGRATION COURT (as of April 1, 2026)
(a) A written motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order, with a cover page and proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA, filed with the immigration court that entered the order (not the BIA). The motion should be based on INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii): he did not receive proper notice of the hearing under INA 239(a)(1) or (2).
- Time limit: none. A lack-of-notice motion may be filed at any time. The 180-day limit in 240(b)(5)(C)(i) applies only to exceptional-circumstances motions, and that ground is probably unavailable because he learned of the order after the 180 days ran.
- Automatic stay: timely filing of a lack-of-notice motion automatically stays removal until the IJ rules, 240(b)(5)(C) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). He should file it before any ICE enforcement action.
- Core argument: the Notice to Appear (NTA) and any hearing notice were mailed to an address he never gave DHS. Written notice goes to the address the noncitizen provides, 239(a)(1) and (a)(2). The 240(b)(5)(A) in absentia order also requires clear, unequivocal, and convincing evidence that written notice was provided and that he is removable. Mailing to an address he never provided is not notice. The in absentia order should be rescinded on that ground.
- Facts to prove: a declaration that he never received the NTA or hearing notice and never lived at, or used, the address; his actual residence history; the I-130/I-485 filings showing the address he did give (the USCIS record shows the same error, so he should show that he never supplied that address, for example through the I-485 and I-130 copies and receipt notices); and proof that he did not move or evade. He should also attach a copy of the DHS NTA and the Certificate of Service, which he can obtain through FOIA, the EOIR ACIS/portal, or a records request.
- Presumption of delivery: ordinary-mail notice carries a rebuttable presumption of delivery that is weaker than for certified mail. Matter of M-R-A-, 24 I&N Dec. 665 (BIA 2008), and Matter of Grijalva, 21 I&N Dec. 27 (BIA 1995), govern rebuttal. Relevant evidence includes a sworn affidavit, diligence in pursuing relief, and the fact that he had pending applications and so had a strong incentive to appear. Pending-application diligence is also the natural explanation for why he did not appear.
- Address-duty caveat: the failure-to-provide-address rule in 239(a)(2)(B) and 240(b)(5)(B) only applies if he was required to provide an address and failed to. If DHS used an address he never provided, he should argue that this rule does not apply. Because the NTA appears to have been mailed to the same faulty USCIS address, he should check whether the NTA also lacked required hearing time and place information, Pereira v. Sessions, 585 U.S. 198 (2018), and Niz-Chavez v. Garland, 593 U.S. 155 (2021). Those cases are not an independent ground to rescind without a notice failure. Under Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), a defective NTA does not bar an in absentia order if a later hearing notice was properly given. So he needs to prove that all notices failed.
- Circuit law: if the case arose in a particular circuit, he should check that circuit's standard for notice and the presumption of delivery.
(b) In the alternative, he can include a fallback request for reopening under 240(b)(5)(C)(i) (exceptional circumstances). That ground is probably untimely, because 180 days from August 1, 2025 ended about January 28, 2026. It carries the H.R. 1 fee, so I would not rely on it. A sua sponte reopening request under 1003.23(b)(1) is another fallback, but it is discretionary, rarely granted, and fee-bearing in general.
(c) A request to reopen to apply for adjustment of status, or the I-485 itself, should be filed with the motion, along with a request to terminate or to administratively close, if the IJ reopens. After reopening, the husband renews his I-485 before the IJ under 8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii) and 1240.1(a)(1)(ii). The adjustment application is made with Form I-485 filed with the court after DHS has decided the I-130 issue, or he can ask the IJ to continue the case while a new or reopened I-130 is adjudicated by USCIS.
(d) He should also file a Form EOIR-33 change of address (and EOIR-28 if represented), so that future notices reach him.

2. FEES
- A motion to reopen an in absentia order based on lack of notice or custody under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii): no fee. This is exempt by 8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)(iii) and remains exempt after H.R. 1 (the 2025 reconciliation law, Pub. L. 119-21).
- The H.R. 1 fee for a motion to reopen or reconsider before an IJ is $900, in addition to the base fee. The base fee is $145, and I could not verify whether the 2025 $110 figure still applies. No fee waiver is available for the $900 fee. The statutory $900 amount is subject to inflation adjustment for FY2026 (EOIR notice published January 21, 2026), and I did not verify the adjusted figure. These fees apply only to the exceptional-circumstances ground or sua sponte requests, not to the lack-of-notice motion.
- If the case is reopened, he would owe the I-485 filing fee ($1,440 as of 2024 USCIS rates, to be confirmed). Whether the I-485 must be paid again to DHS or the court should be checked. Biometrics may also be required. USCIS fees are not paid to the court. I did not verify the current USCIS I-485 fee, or whether he would owe a new fee.
- If the I-485 is refiled with the court, the IJ practice guidance says the application and fee receipt from USCIS are needed. I did not verify this.

3. CONTESTING THE I-130 AND I-485 DENIALS
- I-130 denial for abandonment (no RFE response, December 5, 2023). No BIA appeal lies from a denial for failure to respond to an RFE (8 CFR 103.2(b)(13), (b)(15)). The 30-day window for a motion to reopen or reconsider under 8 CFR 103.5 has long expired. An untimely motion to reopen is excusable only if the delay was reasonable and beyond the petitioner's control (103.5(a)(1)(i)), which is a stretch after more than two years, but the wrong-address error by USCIS is a strong equity. The better route is to file a new I-130 with the evidence (and a copy of the RFE), or to ask USCIS to reopen on its own motion because the RFE went to a wrong address. The wife's I-130 is for an immediate relative and has no visa-number limit. Reapplying does not involve a new fee beyond the I-130 fee. Notice that USCIS error in mailing to an address never given is the key argument.
- I-485 denial (January 15, 2024). Because the I-130 was denied, the I-485 was denied as a consequence. No appeal lies from an I-485 denial (8 CFR 103.3(a)(1)(iii)). A motion to reopen with USCIS is also long untimely. However, once removal proceedings begin, USCIS no longer has jurisdiction over a renewed I-485; the IJ does (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)(i), (a)(5)(ii)). The IJ can review the I-485 de novo if the order is rescinded.
- Adjustment eligibility issues to anticipate: he entered on a B-2 visa and married 19 days later. DHS may argue preconceived intent or misrepresentation, 22 CFR 40.63 (the 90-day rule, applied by analogy; it is guidance for consular officers only), INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i), and bona fides of the marriage, INA 204(c) is not implicated unless there was a prior fraud finding. He is an immediate relative of a US citizen, so unlawful presence and overstay do not bar adjustment under INA 245(a) and (c) (immediate relatives are exempt from the 245(c) bars). He was admitted and inspected, and his I-94 expired June 1, 2023, after the I-485 was filed, so he was in lawful status when the application was filed.
- Also consider: a federal court action under the APA and 8 USC 1329 or mandamus against USCIS is possible but weak (the I-485 denial is the final agency action, and the limitations period under 28 USC 2401(a) is six years). Judicial review of the in absentia order is by petition for review within 30 days of the order (INA 242(b)(1)) and is limited to the validity of notice and the removability findings (INA 242(b)(5)), so it is not available now. A motion to reopen is the proper route. If the IJ denies the motion, he should appeal to the BIA within 30 days (8 CFR 1003.38(b)) and file a petition for review in the court of appeals.

4. PRACTICAL STEPS
(1) Retain counsel immediately and file the motion without delay to trigger the automatic stay. (2) File EOIR-33. (3) Request the A-file and record of proceedings (FOIA/ROP). (4) File a new I-130 and request expedited handling. (5) Prepare the I-485 with the motion.

CAVEATS. My fee and statutory points come from secondary summaries found by search; the official sources (eCFR, EOIR memos, Cornell LII) were blocked by the network proxy and I could not open them. The exact current fee amounts for April 2026 should be confirmed on the EOIR fee page. Some specifics in this answer, such as the I-485 fee, the base motion fee, and some case and regulation pin cites, come from background knowledge and are unverified.

issues.text: Motion to reopen in absentia order for lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii): no deadline, automatic stay, and the standard for rebutting the presumption of delivery
Fees: lack-of-notice motion is fee-exempt; the H.R.1 $900 fee applies to other reopening grounds
Recourse against the I-130 abandonment denial and I-485 denial: no appeal, the 103.5 motion deadline has passed, a new I-130 can be filed, and the I-485 can be renewed before the IJ
Adjustment eligibility risks: marriage shortly after B-2 entry, preconceived intent, misrepresentation

claims.text: A motion to reopen based on lack of notice can be filed at any time, automatically stays removal, and is the primary route to challenge the in absentia order
That motion has no filing fee, even after H.R. 1; the $900 plus base fee applies to other reopening motions
The I-130/I-485 denials cannot be directly appealed; the remedy is a new I-130 and renewal of the I-485 before the IJ if proceedings are reopened
He must rebut the presumption of delivery with evidence that the notice address was never provided
